## Building the installed cost from unit costs

**Step 1 — thermal capacity → salt mass**
Two-tank molten (solar) salt system, 60/40 NaNO₃/KNO₃, ΔT = 565°C (hot) − 290°C (cold) = 275 K, Cp ≈ 1.52 kJ/kg·K, mean density ≈ 1,800 kg/m³.

- Energy density = Cp·ΔT = 418 kJ/kg = 0.116 kWh/kg
- Salt mass for 5,000 kWh = 5,000 / 0.116 ≈ **43 tonnes**
- Volume ≈ 24 m³; each tank must hold the *full* inventory (salt moves entirely between tanks), so two tanks × ~29 m³ (with freeboard) ≈ **58 m³ of tankage**

**Step 2 — unit costs**

| Item | Basis | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Salt | 43 t × $900/t | $39,000 |
| Two insulated/refractory-lined tanks | 58 m³ × $4,000/m³ (small-batch, not mass-produced) | $232,000 |
| Charge-side heat exchanger (electric immersion heater) | 625 kWth × $200/kW | $125,000 |
| Discharge-side heat exchanger (salt→process fluid) | 833 kWth × $400/kW | $333,000 |
| Salt pumps (hot + cold leg, specialty 321H SS) | 2 units | $120,000 |
| Salt-rated piping & valves | — | $80,000 |
| Freeze-protection trace heating (salt freezes ~220°C) | — | $30,000 |
| Instrumentation & controls | — | $40,000 |
| **Equipment subtotal** | | **≈$1.0M** |
| EPC install wrap (structural, electrical, labor) | 35% of equipment | $350,000 |
| Engineering/PM/commissioning/contingency | 20% of (equip+install) | $270,000 |
| **Installed total** | | **≈$1.62M** |

**Installed cost ≈ $320/kWh of thermal storage capacity.**

The dominant line items aren't the salt (4% of cost) — they're the heat exchangers, pumps, and controls, which don't scale down. That's the key first-principles insight: at *utility* scale (hundreds of MWh, e.g. Gemasolar/Crescent Dunes), published two-tank molten-salt TES costs run $20–40/kWh thermal, because those fixed-ticket items (one set of pumps, one set of HX, one control system) amortize over a vastly larger salt mass. At 5 MWh, the same fixed items get divided by almost nothing, so cost per kWh is ~10x higher. This is a strongly scale-dependent technology.

## Amortizing over cycle life

Molten salt itself barely degrades; tanks/pumps/HX are good for ~25–30 years. At 1 cycle/day, 95% availability:

- Cycles over 30 yr ≈ 10,400
- **Capital cost per kWh of *heat* delivered** = $1.62M / (5,000 kWh × 10,400 cycles) ≈ **3.1 ¢/kWh_th** (+~1–2¢ O&M → ~4–5¢/kWh_th all-in)

If that heat is instead routed through a power block to make electricity (~35–40% thermal→electric efficiency is typical for small-scale cycles), the *storage* cost alone per kWh_e delivered becomes:

- 5,000 kWh_th × 0.35 = 1,750 kWh_e per cycle
- $1.62M / (1,750 × 10,400) ≈ **8.9 ¢/kWh_e** — and that excludes the turbine/generator capex entirely, which at this tiny ~800 kWe scale would add a comparable or larger sum.

## Lithium-ion comparison

Utility-scale Li-ion BESS, installed ≈ $280/kWh, ~5,000 cycles @ 80% DoD, ~92% round-trip efficiency:

- $280 / (5,000 × 0.92) ≈ **6.1 ¢/kWh_e** (capital only)

## Verdict

- **As direct heat storage**, molten-salt TES isn't really competing with Li-ion at all — Li-ion can't deliver heat without its own conversion losses — and at 3–5 ¢/kWh_th it's cheap in absolute terms despite the high nominal $/kWh capacity cost, purely because of the 2–3x longer cycle life.
- **As an electricity-storage asset at 5 MWh**, molten salt loses decisively to Li-ion (≈9 ¢/kWh_e for storage alone, before adding power-block capex, vs ≈6 ¢/kWh_e all-in for Li-ion), because the round-trip efficiency penalty (35–40% vs 92%) outweighs the cycle-life advantage, and the fixed-cost items are crushing at this scale.
- The crossover is scale, not chemistry: molten salt only becomes electricity-storage-competitive once it's sharing a power block and amortizing fixed costs across on the order of 100+ MWh (i.e., CSP-plant scale), not a 5 MWh unit.
